_fieldConventions.eco: ECO code (Encyclopaedia of Chess Openings), string. Source of record: lichess-org/chess-openings dataset (CC0), Wikipedia ECO table as fallback.
_fieldConventions.name: Opening name, string.
_fieldConventions.color: Which side this entry represents/owns: 'White' or 'Black'.
_fieldConventions.pgn: Canonical move sequence reaching this opening, in SAN.
_fieldConventions.depthOfTheory: Hard filter. One of 'Shallow' | 'Moderate' | 'Deep'. One value per entry — an opening family spanning multiple depths is represented by multiple entries at different ECO codes, not a range on one entry.
_fieldConventions.timeControls: Hard filter. Array of eligible values from ['Bullet/Blitz', 'Rapid', 'Classical/Correspondence'].
_fieldConventions.ratingBand: Soft-scored. Integer 1-5, matching the user rating taxonomy: 1=Beginner, 2=Intermediate, 3=Advanced, 4=Expert, 5=Master. Compared via distance against the user's own band value.

style.tacticalVsPositional: Soft-scored. Integer -2..+2. -2 = strongly positional, +2 = strongly tactical.
style.riskTolerance: Soft-scored. Integer -2..+2. -2 = very solid/safe, +2 = very sharp/gambit-friendly.
style.dynamicVsStatic: Soft-scored. Integer -2..+2. -2 = strongly static (stable structures), +2 = strongly dynamic (imbalanced, initiative-chasing structures).
style.forgivingVsPunishing: Soft-scored. Integer -2..+2. -2 = very forgiving (mistakes stay recoverable), +2 = very punishing (one inaccuracy can be immediately losing).

_fieldConventions.healthAtHigherLevels: Soft-scored (drives the Longevity criterion). Integer -2..+2. -2 = known to be dubious/refuted against strong opposition, +2 = a mainstay even at elite level. Not a boolean — graded to avoid forcing an all-or-nothing 'is this bad' call.
_fieldConventions.estimatedHoursToCompetency: Not filtered or scored directly. Divided by the user's daily study-time budget to personalize the rationale line (e.g. 'about 2 weeks at your pace').

openings.name: Dutch Defense
openings.overview: The Dutch Defense answers 1.d4 with 1...f5, staking an early claim on e4 and preparing kingside activity at the cost of a small permanent weakness on the e8-h5 diagonal in front of Black's own king. It produces the lowest draw rate of any of the common replies to 1.d4, since it commits Black to unbalanced, fighting positions rather than symmetrical equality, and it splits into sharply different characters depending on Black's setup — from the hypermodern fianchetto systems of the Leningrad Variation to the locked, static center of the Stonewall. First recommended in print by Elias Stein in 1789, it was dismissed as unsound by Siegbert Tarrasch in 1931 but has been rehabilitated many times since.
openings.reputationNotes: It has never been a true main line against 1.d4 and is rarely seen at the very top today, but it has attracted a genuinely strong list of practitioners over the decades — Alekhine, Larsen, Najdorf, and more recently Nakamura and Carlsen (especially in Stonewall setups) — and remains entirely viable at club and master level alike.

openings.name: Scandinavian Defense
openings.overview: The Scandinavian Defense (or Center Counter, 1.e4 d5) strikes at White's e-pawn immediately, forcing matters in the center on move one; after 2.exd5, Black chooses between recapturing at once with 2...Qxd5 (accepting an early loss of time when White plays 3.Nc3) or the Modern Scandinavian, 2...Nf6, which delays the recapture to avoid that tempo loss altogether. It is one of the oldest documented openings in chess, appearing in a 15th-century poem describing a game with the modern queen and bishop moves.
openings.reputationNotes: Long treated as a slightly passive, second-tier option next to the French or Caro-Kann, it has been steadily rehabilitated since Bent Larsen's win over Anatoly Karpov in 1979 and now enjoys genuine elite respectability — Magnus Carlsen in particular has used it repeatedly to beat and draw top-level opposition, including at classical and blitz world championship level.

openings.name: Caro-Kann Defense
openings.overview: The Caro-Kann meets 1.e4 with 1...c6, preparing to challenge the center with ...d5 while, unlike the French Defense, keeping the light-squared bishop free to develop outside the pawn chain before the structure locks up. Play typically continues 2.d4 d5, after which White chooses between the main 3.Nc3/3.Nd2 lines, the space-grabbing 3.e5 Advance Variation, or the simplifying 3.exd5 Exchange Variation. It is one of the most solid and reliable answers to 1.e4, trading a small loss of time for a resilient structure with few lasting weaknesses.
openings.reputationNotes: Long known as a slightly passive but rock-solid choice, it has been rehabilitated as a fully fashionable top-level weapon in the hands of players such as Alireza Firouzja and Ding Liren, and remains an excellent, low-maintenance choice at club level too.

openings.name: Najdorf Sicilian
openings.overview: The Najdorf is the most studied and arguably most prestigious branch of the entire Sicilian complex: 5...a6 is a subtle, flexible move that rules out Bb5+ checks and keeps every option open — ...e5, ...e6, a fianchetto, queenside expansion with ...b5 — before Black commits to a specific structure. Both sides typically play for a full-blooded fight with chances to attack on opposite wings, making it the definitive vehicle for players who want maximal winning chances with either color.
openings.reputationNotes: Made famous above all by Bobby Fischer and Garry Kasparov, who both used it as a primary weapon for most of their careers, it remains the single deepest-theory main line in the entire Sicilian Defense — a lifetime study for those who take it up seriously, and a line where memorized preparation matters enormously even at club level.

openings.name: Italian Game (Giuoco Piano)
openings.overview: A classical and direct opening where White develops the kingside bishop to c4, exerting pressure on f7 and the kingside. Black has numerous flexible responses, making it a popular choice at all levels.
openings.reputationNotes: A classical and popular opening at all levels; slightly more aggressive than the Ruy Lopez, it leads to rich middlegame play with chances for both sides.

openings.name: Ruy Lopez (Spanish Opening)
openings.overview: The most popular and theoretically important of all Open Games, where White's bishop on b5 exerts immediate pressure on Black's position. Extensively analyzed with countless variations, it remains the choice of world champions at all levels.
openings.reputationNotes: The most respected and widely played opening at the highest levels; used by world champions, it offers White excellent practical chances with rich, complex positions.

openings.name: French Defense
openings.overview: A solid and popular defense against 1.e4 where Black plays 1...e6 and 2...d5, creating a strong pawn chain in the center. Black accepts a slight space disadvantage but gains a very stable position with good counterplay.
openings.reputationNotes: A highly respected and solid defense at all levels; while Black gets a cramped position, the solid structure and available counterplay make it a world championship weapon.

openings.name: Scotch Game
openings.overview: A classical and aggressive opening where White plays 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4, challenging Black's center immediately. It leads to open, tactical positions with clear piece play and good winning chances for White.
openings.reputationNotes: A classical and sound opening with recent resurgence in popularity; offers White more direct play than other main lines with clear winning opportunities.
